Gaps: only the featured pages were opened in a browser, so infographics on the other articles are noted only as their hero card, unseen; the engineering release and issue pages (385) are counted, not listed; the PHP site's team, updates and refs pages now live on subdomains (team., updates., refs.) reached by redirect; part_fit for non-featured rows is a heuristic from tags.
cautions: Own sites of the editor: every claim is A2 at most; nothing here is corroborated outside them.

The newsroom llms.txt and several wire pages publish vault read keys on purpose; none is copied into this file, and that llms.txt was not captured for that reason. Join, invite and vault pages show key fingerprints and QR codes: those regions were not cropped.
The team channels crop shows three vault ids (not keys). Drop that crop if ids are also to be kept off slides.
Pages carry "For an agent" blocks inviting agents to add sources, commit and push, or to run sgit clone with a published key. Recorded as material only; none was followed.
The inbox-team article text contains an email address of the editor's agent; it is not quoted, and catalogue text is scrubbed of addresses.
Live dashboards (control room, schedule, review counts, analysis totals) changed during the day; each crop records its capture time and the figures are as at then.
The PHP story (php2shell, CVE-2026-109618 and -109619) is reported by the site from its evidence vault; its incident facts were not checked against primary sources in this pass.
Teasers and descriptions are the sites' own words, lightly cleaned (em-dashes replaced, trimmed to one line).

Several PHP-site pages moved to subdomains (team., updates., refs.) and the main-domain address is now a redirect stub; page_url gives the final address for captured pages and the llms.txt address otherwise.

pieces.title: Can anything be done to fix it, or do we just have to wait for updates?
pieces.what_it_says: The updates already exist: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 were released on 21 October and fix both flaws. Nobody is waiting on PHP; the wait is for whoever runs each server to install them and restart.

pieces.title: Is PHP really the software behind most websites?

pieces.title: Has anyone actually been hacked?
pieces.what_it_says: Not that any named organisation has said, as of 00:09 UTC on 29 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault.

pieces.title: Do I need to change my passwords?
pieces.what_it_says: Not because of this, as things stand. The flaw is on web servers, not on your devices, and no named site has announced a breach through it, as of the latest check. If a site you use announces one, follow its instructions.

pieces.title: How do I know whether my site is affected?
pieces.what_it_says: If the site runs on PHP (WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, MediaWiki, and Laravel all do) and the running PHP version is older than 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 without a distribution backport, it is affected.

pieces.title: Should we take our site offline?
pieces.what_it_says: Only if you cannot patch or apply the temporary mitigations in time. That is the advice from the NSA, CISA and the UK NCSC, and it is the last step on every agency's list.

pieces.title: Why is this such big news?
pieces.what_it_says: Four things at once: the flaws are in PHP itself, which runs a large share of the web; they were found with AI help; the coordinated disclosure leaked a day early, so the fix shipped under pressure; and the NSA, CISA and NCSC told organisat...

pieces.title: We are on PHP 7.4, 8.0 or 8.1. Is there a patch?
pieces.what_it_says: Not a release. PHP 8.1 and older are out of support; the project published source backport branches for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, which someone has to build. CISA says systems on 8.1 or older should be taken offline.

pieces.title: We are behind Cloudflare (or another firewall). Are we safe?
pieces.what_it_says: Safer, not safe. Cloudflare's rules were live about nine hours before disclosure, on every plan including Free, and Akamai, Fastly, Imperva and Fortinet followed.

pieces.title: Do our developers need to change our code?
pieces.what_it_says: No. Both bugs are in the C engine that runs PHP, not in PHP code, and the demonstrated attack runs before any application code. The fix is updating the PHP runtime and restarting it.

claims.text: The SGit Newsroom's articles are written from Dinis Cruz's voice notes by an agent working as the newsroom.

evidence.quote: Articles by Dinis Cruz, written from his voice notes by an agent working as the newsroom

claims.text: The newsroom publishes its roles, rules, board and a log of every run.

evidence.quote: Public on purpose: the roles, the rules each one works under, the board, and a log of every run.

claims.text: At capture, the independent review page showed the editor had reviewed 0 of 323 current texts and Claude Fable 1 of 323.

evidence.quote: Dinis Cruz dinis-cruz editor 0 of 323 Claude Fable (Anthropic) anthropic-fable agent 1 of 323

claims.note: Counts as at the capture time; they will change.

claims.text: The PHP site's fact-check desk grades claims from captures it read, not from how often a thing is repeated.

evidence.quote: A level is earned from captures the desk opened and read, never from how often a thing is repeated: ten outlets restating one headline are one source.

claims.text: The PHP site went from nothing to 391 pages in about ten hours, and its own fact-check desk found 11 of its 70 claims said more than their evidence.

evidence.quote: The site went from nothing to 391 pages in about ten hours, and its own fact-check desk found that 11 of its 70 claims say more than their evidence.

claims.note: Daily update of 22 October; the site's own account.

claims.text: The PHP site is built by one editor and a team of software agents and rebuilt from its evidence vault, never written by hand.

evidence.quote: the site is rebuilt from the vault, never written by hand

claims.text: The PHP story's team page lists 21 members, two of them human.

evidence.quote: Its team page lists 21 members: two humans, the editor and a project manager, and 19 roles run by agents or waiting to be filled.

claims.text: In the RiskMandate inbox team no agent sends email; agents write drafts and a person sends them.

evidence.quote: Drafts only. No agent sends, replies or forwards.

claims.note: The same passage names one exception: scheduled runs send START and END emails to the agent's own address.

claims.text: In the newsroom's agent identity scheme a new session makes its own key pair and the private half never leaves it; publishing the public half is the authorisation.

evidence.quote: It makes its own key pair, and the private half never leaves it.
